claim: Mammalian cerebral cortex is accepted as being critical for voluntary motor control.
source: Mammalian cerebral cortex is accepted as being critical for voluntary motor control, but what functions depend on cortex is still unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific consensus in the abstract.

claim: The specific functions of cortex in voluntary motor control are still unclear.
source: Mammalian cerebral cortex is accepted as being critical for voluntary motor control, but what functions depend on cortex is still unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Sudden cortical inhibition blocked initiation of skilled prehension behavior.
source: Sudden cortical inhibition blocked initiation or froze execution of this skilled prehension behavior, but left untrained forelimb movements unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Sudden cortical inhibition froze execution of skilled prehension behavior.
source: Sudden cortical inhibition blocked initiation or froze execution of this skilled prehension behavior, but left untrained forelimb movements unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Sudden cortical inhibition left untrained forelimb movements unaffected.
source: Sudden cortical inhibition blocked initiation or froze execution of this skilled prehension behavior, but left untrained forelimb movements unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Kinematically normal prehension occurred immediately after cortical inhibition.
source: Unexpectedly, kinematically normal prehension occurred immediately after cortical inhibition, even during rest periods lacking cue and pellet.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Rebound prehension occurred even during rest periods lacking cue and pellet.
source: Unexpectedly, kinematically normal prehension occurred immediately after cortical inhibition, even during rest periods lacking cue and pellet.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Rebound prehension was only evoked in trained animals.
source: This 'rebound' prehension was only evoked in trained and food-deprived animals, suggesting that a motivation-gated motor engram sufficient to evoke prehension is activated at inhibition's end.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Rebound prehension was only evoked in food-deprived animals.
source: This 'rebound' prehension was only evoked in trained and food-deprived animals, suggesting that a motivation-gated motor engram sufficient to evoke prehension is activated at inhibition's end.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: A motivation-gated motor engram sufficient to evoke prehension is activated at inhibition's end.
source: This 'rebound' prehension was only evoked in trained and food-deprived animals, suggesting that a motivation-gated motor engram sufficient to evoke prehension is activated at inhibition's end.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Cortical activity is necessary for enacting a learned skill.
source: These results demonstrate the necessity and sufficiency of cortical activity for enacting a learned skill.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the abstract.

claim: Cortical activity is sufficient for enacting a learned skill.
source: These results demonstrate the necessity and sufficiency of cortical activity for enacting a learned skill.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the abstract.

claim: Motor control is achieved by the coordinated activity of cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, cerebellum, and spinal cord.
source: Motor control is achieved by the coordinated activity of myriad neural structures, including the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, cerebellum, and spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Cortical neurons display dynamic activity patterns during movement planning and execution.
source: Cortical neurons display dynamic activity patterns during movement planning and execution, but their functional contribution to skilled action cannot be assessed from recordings alone (Lemon, 1993; Scott, 2003; Evarts, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The functional contribution of cortical neurons to skilled action cannot be assessed from recordings alone.
source: Cortical neurons display dynamic activity patterns during movement planning and execution, but their functional contribution to skilled action cannot be assessed from recordings alone (Lemon, 1993; Scott, 2003; Evarts, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous inactivation experiments have suggested the cortex tunes motor programs to achieve dexterous movement.
source: Previous inactivation experiments have suggested the cortex tunes—rather than initiates and executes—motor programs to achieve dexterous movement (Walker and Fulton, 1938; Lawrence and Kuypers, 1968; Castro, 1972; Passingham et al., 1983; Martin and Ghez, 1991; Whishaw, 2000; Fogassi et al., 2001; Peters et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous inactivation experiments suggested the cortex does not initiate motor programs to achieve dexterous movement.
source: Previous inactivation experiments have suggested the cortex tunes—rather than initiates and executes—motor programs to achieve dexterous movement (Walker and Fulton, 1938; Lawrence and Kuypers, 1968; Castro, 1972; Passingham et al., 1983; Martin and Ghez, 1991; Whishaw, 2000; Fogassi et al., 2001; Peters et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous inactivation experiments suggested the cortex does not execute motor programs to achieve dexterous movement.
source: Previous inactivation experiments have suggested the cortex tunes—rather than initiates and executes—motor programs to achieve dexterous movement (Walker and Fulton, 1938; Lawrence and Kuypers, 1968; Castro, 1972; Passingham et al., 1983; Martin and Ghez, 1991; Whishaw, 2000; Fogassi et al., 2001; Peters et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Classical perturbation methods lack temporal specificity.
source: The classical perturbation methods used in these studies lack temporal specificity and allow for the emergence of compensatory mechanisms (but see supplement of Peters et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a critique of previous methods with citation support.

claim: Classical perturbation methods allow for the emergence of compensatory mechanisms.
source: The classical perturbation methods used in these studies lack temporal specificity and allow for the emergence of compensatory mechanisms (but see supplement of Peters et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a critique of previous methods with citation support.

claim: Electrical stimulation of cortex has been shown to be sufficient to elicit complex movements.
source: Electrical stimulation of cortex has been shown to be sufficient to elicit complex movements, but it remains difficult to resolve if evoked behaviors are caused by direct cortical neuron stimulation or antidromic activation of inputs to cortex (Ferrier, 1873; Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Penfield, 1954; Gottlieb et al., 1993; Graziano et al., 2002; Ramanathan et al., 2006; Harrison et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It remains difficult to resolve if evoked behaviors from electrical stimulation are caused by direct cortical neuron stimulation or antidromic activation of inputs to cortex.
source: Electrical stimulation of cortex has been shown to be sufficient to elicit complex movements, but it remains difficult to resolve if evoked behaviors are caused by direct cortical neuron stimulation or antidromic activation of inputs to cortex (Ferrier, 1873; Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Penfield, 1954; Gottlieb et al., 1993; Graziano et al., 2002; Ramanathan et al., 2006; Harrison et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a limitation of previous methods supported by citations.

claim: The precise role of cortex in skilled movement remains unclear.
source: Thus the precise role of cortex in skilled movement remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: The authors developed a multi-step, cued, prehension task in which head-fixed mice reach for a food pellet, grab it, and bring the pellet to the mouth for consumption.
source: To test the role of the cortex for control of skilled motor tasks, we developed a multi-step, cued, prehension task in which head-fixed mice reach for a food pellet, grab it, and bring the pellet to the mouth for consumption (Figure 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with reference to Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Prehension behavior was broken down into six sequential epochs: Lift, Hand open, Grab, Supinate, At mouth, and Chew.
source: This prehension behavior was broken down into six sequential epochs (Lift, Hand open, Grab, Supinate, At mouth, and Chew; Figure 1B and C) that divide the complex movement into components that involve distinct muscle activations.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with reference to Figure 1B and C.

claim: The six sequential epochs of prehension divide the complex movement into components that involve distinct muscle activations.
source: This prehension behavior was broken down into six sequential epochs (Lift, Hand open, Grab, Supinate, At mouth, and Chew; Figure 1B and C) that divide the complex movement into components that involve distinct muscle activations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental design with reference to Figure 1B and C.

claim: The task employed head fixation to reduce postural variability.
source: Unlike previous paradigms, our task employed head fixation to reduce postural variability, allow examination of reaction time, and enable future physiological investigations (Whishaw et al., 1991; Osborne and Dudman, 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design with citation support.

claim: The task employed head fixation to allow examination of reaction time.
source: Unlike previous paradigms, our task employed head fixation to reduce postural variability, allow examination of reaction time, and enable future physiological investigations (Whishaw et al., 1991; Osborne and Dudman, 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design with citation support.

claim: The task employed head fixation to enable future physiological investigations.
source: Unlike previous paradigms, our task employed head fixation to reduce postural variability, allow examination of reaction time, and enable future physiological investigations (Whishaw et al., 1991; Osborne and Dudman, 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design with citation support.

claim: All animals that underwent training learned the task.
source: All animals that underwent training learned the task.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: Reaching for the pellet could be achieved in 5–10 sessions.
source: Reaching for the pellet could be achieved in 5–10 sessions and stable performance (median success rate was 74%, n = 13 animals) could be realized in approximately 15 sessions.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: Stable performance with a median success rate of 74% could be realized in approximately 15 sessions.
source: Reaching for the pellet could be achieved in 5–10 sessions and stable performance (median success rate was 74%, n = 13 animals) could be realized in approximately 15 sessions.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=13 animals.

claim: The authors used high-speed video and machine-learning-based tracking to semi-automatically convert filmed movements into hand trajectories.
source: We used high-speed video and machine-learning-based tracking to semi-automatically convert filmed movements into hand trajectories (see Materials and methods, Figure 1D and E, Video 2).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with reference to Figure 1D and E, and Video 2.

claim: Head-fixed prehension shows stereotypy in sequential trajectories from a single animal during a behavioral session.
source: Stereotypy of head-fixed prehension can be seen in sequential trajectories from a single animal during a behavioral session (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The authors employed rapid onset, within-trial suppression by light-activating channelrhodopsin (ChR2)-expressing inhibitory neurons in cortex.
source: To avoid this confound, we employed rapid onset, within-trial suppression by light-activating channelrhodopsin (ChR2)-expressing inhibitory neurons (expressing the vesicular GABA transporter [Slc32a1]) in cortex with pulses of light (Figure 2) (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with reference to Figure 2 and citation.

claim: ChR2-expressing inhibitory neurons express the vesicular GABA transporter (Slc32a1).
source: To avoid this confound, we employed rapid onset, within-trial suppression by light-activating channelrhodopsin (ChR2)-expressing inhibitory neurons (expressing the vesicular GABA transporter [Slc32a1]) in cortex with pulses of light (Figure 2) (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with citation support.

claim: Cortical inhibition was limited in space by regulating the position of light exposure.
source: Cortical inhibition was limited in space (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and time by regulating the position and duration of light exposure.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cortical inhibition was limited in time by regulating the duration of light exposure.
source: Cortical inhibition was limited in space (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and time by regulating the position and duration of light exposure.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Light was delivered on less than 20% of trials during a behavioral session to limit compensation.
source: To limit compensation, light was delivered on less than 20% of trials during a behavioral session.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The only effective area of cortical suppression for blocking prehension initiation was centered over contralateral forelimb motor cortex.
source: We first applied inhibition at cue onset to test the role of cortex for behavior initiation. The only effective area of cortical suppression was centered over contralateral forelimb motor cortex (Figure 2B–E, Video 3).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 2B–E and Video 3.

claim: Forelimb motor and sensory cortices are overlapping at this resolution in the rodent.
source: Because forelimb motor and sensory cortices are overlapping at this resolution in the rodent, we will refer to this region as sensorimotor (SM) cortex (Ayling et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Contralateral sensorimotor cortex suppression at the beginning of an individual trial eliminated initiation of the prehension behavior in 35 of 459 trials.
source: Contralateral sensorimotor cortex suppression at the beginning of an individual trial eliminated initiation of the prehension behavior (initiation only occurred in 35 of 459 trials during contralateral sensorimotor cortex inhibition, compared to initiation in 3675 of 3692 control trials, n = 8 animals, Figure 2A and B, Video 3).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=8 animals and reference to Figure 2A and B, and Video 3.

claim: In control trials, prehension initiation occurred in 3675 of 3692 trials.
source: Contralateral sensorimotor cortex suppression at the beginning of an individual trial eliminated initiation of the prehension behavior (initiation only occurred in 35 of 459 trials during contralateral sensorimotor cortex inhibition, compared to initiation in 3675 of 3692 control trials, n = 8 animals, Figure 2A and B, Video 3).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=8 animals and reference to Figure 2A and B, and Video 3.

claim: Prehension reliably occurred after optogenetic cortical suppression was relinquished in 436 of 467 trials.
source: Prehension reliably occurred after optogenetic cortical suppression was relinquished (initiation in 436 of 467 trials, n = 8 animals), Figure 2B, Video 3).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=8 animals and reference to Figure 2B and Video 3.

claim: Inhibition of ipsilateral sensorimotor cortex did not affect behavioral initiation rates (initiation in 124 of 124 trials).
source: Inhibition of other cortical areas did not affect behavioral initiation rates (ipsilateral sensorimotor (initiation in 124 of 124 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 2C, Video 4), visual (initiation in 122 of 124 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 2D), and frontal (initiation in 124 of 124 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 2E) cortex).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=3 animals and reference to Figure 2C and Video 4.

claim: Inhibition of visual cortex did not affect behavioral initiation rates (initiation in 122 of 124 trials).
source: Inhibition of other cortical areas did not affect behavioral initiation rates (ipsilateral sensorimotor (initiation in 124 of 124 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 2C, Video 4), visual (initiation in 122 of 124 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 2D), and frontal (initiation in 124 of 124 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 2E) cortex).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=3 animals and reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Inhibition of frontal cortex did not affect behavioral initiation rates (initiation in 124 of 124 trials).
source: Inhibition of other cortical areas did not affect behavioral initiation rates (ipsilateral sensorimotor (initiation in 124 of 124 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 2C, Video 4), visual (initiation in 122 of 124 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 2D), and frontal (initiation in 124 of 124 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 2E) cortex).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=3 animals and reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Voluntary grooming was not impacted by sensorimotor cortical suppression (11/11 trials).
source: In contrast to prehension, voluntary grooming was not impacted by sensorimotor cortical suppression (11/11 trials, n = 4 animals, Video 5).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=4 animals and reference to Video 5.

claim: Cued licking behavior was not affected by sensorimotor inhibition.
source: To rule out that initiation failure was due to an inability to process the cue, we activated cortical inhibitory neurons during a cued licking task in which a pellet of food positioned close to the mouth was captured by the tongue; this behavior was not affected by sensorimotor inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Videos 6 and 7.

claim: During the cued licking task, animals sometimes moved their forelimb from the perch to their mouth/table (2/3 animals).
source: During this cued licking task, animals sometimes moved their forelimb from the perch to their mouth/table (2/3 animals, Video 6).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Video 6.

claim: Forelimb movements during cued licking were not kinematically stereotyped.
source: While these movements shared some features with the trained prehension behavior, they were not kinematically stereotyped.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Contralateral sensorimotor cortical suppression did not prevent forelimb movements during cued licking (forelimb movement in 44/44 control trials and 20/20 laser trials for two animals).
source: Contralateral sensorimotor cortical suppression did not prevent these forelimb movements during cued licking (forelimb movement in 44/44 control trials and 20/20 laser trials for two animals, Video 7).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Video 7.

claim: Contralateral sensorimotor cortex activity is necessary for initiation of a learned, goal-directed, skilled prehension behavior.
source: These results indicate that contralateral sensorimotor cortex activity is necessary for initiation of a learned, goal-directed, skilled prehension behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Sensorimotor cortical suppression during the Lift, Hand open, Grab, and Supination components resulted in a freezing of progression towards the target after a short latency (5/5 animals).
source: Sensorimotor cortical suppression during the Lift, Hand open, Grab, and Supination components of the movement resulted in a "freezing" of progression towards the target, after a short latency (5/5 animals; Figure 3A–D; Videos 8, 9, 10, 12 and 16).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=5 animals and reference to Figure 3A–D and Videos 8, 9, 10, 12 and 16.

claim: The latency to freezing was between 72–170 ms for a representative animal.
source: The latency to freezing (between 72–170 ms for a representative animal) implies that this is the timescale over which the cortex commands specific components of the movement (Figure 3A4–D4).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 3A4–D4.

claim: The latency to freezing implies that 72–170 ms is the timescale over which the cortex commands specific components of the movement.
source: The latency to freezing (between 72–170 ms for a representative animal) implies that this is the timescale over which the cortex commands specific components of the movement (Figure 3A4–D4).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings with reference to Figure 3A4–D4.

claim: Movement during the delay was not simply the result of momentum, since in many cases the movement progressed to the next distinct component before freezing.
source: Movement during the delay was not simply the result of momentum, since in many cases the movement progressed to the next distinct component before freezing (Figure 3A3–E4).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings with reference to Figure 3A3–E4.

claim: Cortical suppression was not effective at impeding hand movements involved in chewing.
source: Cortical suppression was not effective at impeding hand movements involved in chewing, suggesting these motor programs do not require sensorimotor cortex (Figure 3E and F, Videos 11 and 13–15), despite involving similar muscle groups.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 3E and F, Videos 11 and 13–15.

claim: Motor programs for chewing do not require sensorimotor cortex.
source: Cortical suppression was not effective at impeding hand movements involved in chewing, suggesting these motor programs do not require sensorimotor cortex (Figure 3E and F, Videos 11 and 13–15), despite involving similar muscle groups.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings with reference to Figure 3E and F, Videos 11 and 13–15.

claim: Prolonged suppression of sensorimotor cortex during freezing resulted in a retraction of the limb either to the perch or a characteristic midair position.
source: Prolonged suppression of sensorimotor cortex during freezing resulted in a retraction of the limb either to the perch or a characteristic midair position (Figure 3A2–E2, Videos 8, 9, 10 and 12).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 3A2–E2, Videos 8, 9, 10 and 12.

claim: Ongoing contralateral sensorimotor cortex activity is necessary for progressing through the steps of a learned, goal-directed, skilled prehension behavior.
source: These results indicate that ongoing contralateral sensorimotor cortex activity is necessary for progressing through the steps of a learned, goal-directed, skilled prehension behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Cortical suppression-induced behavioral freezing was rapidly reversible.
source: Cortical suppression-induced behavioral freezing was rapidly reversible; immediately upon cessation of the light, animals again reached/grabbed for the pellet ("rebound prehension", 8/8 animals, Figure 2B, Figure 3A1–E1, Videos 3, 8–10, 12 and 16).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=8 animals and reference to Figure 2B, Figure 3A1–E1, Videos 3, 8–10, 12 and 16.

claim: Immediately upon cessation of the light, animals again reached/grabbed for the pellet (rebound prehension, 8/8 animals).
source: Cortical suppression-induced behavioral freezing was rapidly reversible; immediately upon cessation of the light, animals again reached/grabbed for the pellet ("rebound prehension", 8/8 animals, Figure 2B, Figure 3A1–E1, Videos 3, 8–10, 12 and 16).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=8 animals and reference to Figure 2B, Figure 3A1–E1, Videos 3, 8–10, 12 and 16.

claim: The initiation of rebound prehension had shorter and less variable latencies when compared to control prehension.
source: The initiation of rebound prehension had shorter and less variable latencies when compared to control (uninterrupted, tone-cued) prehension (Figure 2A and B, 4A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 2A and B, 4A.

claim: Durations of the distinct phases of rebound prehension were not statistically different from control behavior.
source: Once initiated, however, durations of the distinct phases of rebound prehension and the trajectories were not statistically different from control behavior (Figure 4A–C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trajectories of rebound prehension were not statistically different from control behavior.
source: Once initiated, however, durations of the distinct phases of rebound prehension and the trajectories were not statistically different from control behavior (Figure 4A–C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: End-point accuracies of control and rebound prehension attempts were similar (4/5 animals).
source: End-point accuracies of control and rebound prehension attempts were similar (4/5 animals, Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney rank sum, p>0.05; for 1/5 animal difference was significant but median end-point error was only 0.74 +/– 0.52 mm (median +/– median absolute deviation); Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4D and E.

claim: For 1/5 animal, the difference in end-point accuracy was significant but median end-point error was only 0.74 +/– 0.52 mm.
source: End-point accuracies of control and rebound prehension attempts were similar (4/5 animals, Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney rank sum, p>0.05; for 1/5 animal difference was significant but median end-point error was only 0.74 +/– 0.52 mm (median +/– median absolute deviation); Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4D and E.

claim: End-point accuracies were similar for rebound prehension attempts beginning from the perch or from a diversity of midair positions (5/5 animals).
source: Interestingly, end-point accuracies were also similar for rebound prehension attempts either beginning from the perch or from a diversity of midair positions (5/5 animals, Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney rank sum, p>0.05; Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4D and E.

claim: Motor programs comparable to natural forms of the behavior follow termination of inhibitory neuron activation in sensorimotor cortex.
source: Therefore, motor programs comparable to natural forms of the behavior follow termination of inhibitory neuron activation in sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Rebound prehension occurred even on cued trials when the animal had already grabbed the pellet.
source: An involuntary nature of rebound prehension was supported by its occurrence even on cued trials when the animal had already grabbed the pellet (Figure 3, Videos 10, 12 and 16).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 3, Videos 10, 12 and 16.

claim: The involuntary nature of rebound prehension is supported by its occurrence even on cued trials when the animal had already grabbed the pellet.
source: An involuntary nature of rebound prehension was supported by its occurrence even on cued trials when the animal had already grabbed the pellet (Figure 3, Videos 10, 12 and 16).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings with reference to Figure 3, Videos 10, 12 and 16.

claim: During uncued experiments without pellet, animals remained motionless during contralateral sensorimotor cortical inhibition.
source: To further test this, we removed both the pellet and the cue to disengage the animal from the task. During these uncued experiments, the animals remained motionless during contralateral sensorimotor cortical inhibition as expected.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: Following light cessation in uncued experiments, animals reached and grabbed at the empty pellet tray (initiation in 192/224 trials, n = 8 animals).
source: Surprisingly, immediately (~250 ms) following light cessation, the animals reached and grabbed at the empty pellet tray (initiation in 192/224 trials, n = 8 animals, Figure 4F, Videos 17).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=8 animals and reference to Figure 4F, Videos 17.

claim: Rebound execution did not occur in untrained animals (3/3 animals).
source: Rebound execution did not occur in untrained animals (3/3 animals) and was specific to prehension; no other type of movement was generated following light termination (n = 1434 trials, n = 5 animals).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=3 animals.

claim: Rebound execution was specific to prehension; no other type of movement was generated following light termination (n = 1434 trials, n = 5 animals).
source: Rebound execution did not occur in untrained animals (3/3 animals) and was specific to prehension; no other type of movement was generated following light termination (n = 1434 trials, n = 5 animals).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=1434 trials and n=5 animals.

claim: If a pellet was in the target position but the animal was not alerted of its presence, cessation of inhibition frequently generated the full reach-grab-eat sequence.
source: If a pellet was in the target position but the animal was not alerted of its presence, cessation of inhibition frequently generated the full reach-grab-eat sequence (Videos 18).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Videos 18.

claim: Rebound prehension is not the result of ongoing sensory information or the animals' remembered behavioral state.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that rebound prehension is not the result of ongoing sensory information or the animals' remembered behavioral state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Termination of inhibitory neuron activation in sensorimotor cortex, in combination with plastic changes induced by training, is sufficient to evoke a complex, learned motor act.
source: Rather, termination of inhibitory neuron activation in sensorimotor cortex, in combination with plastic changes induced by training, is sufficient to evoke a complex, learned motor act.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: No area outside of sensorimotor cortex contralateral to the utilized limb was effective in evoking rebound prehension in the no cue/no pellet condition.
source: Rebound prehension showed dependence on a number of factors. Anatomically, no area outside of sensorimotor cortex contralateral to the utilized limb was effective in evoking the behavior in the no cue/no pellet condition (ipsilateral sensorimotor, 0/68 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 4G; frontal, 0/20 trials, n = 2 animals; visual, 0/21 trials, n = 3 animals).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 4G.

claim: Inhibition of ipsilateral sensorimotor cortex did not evoke rebound prehension (0/68 trials, n = 3 animals).
source: Rebound prehension showed dependence on a number of factors. Anatomically, no area outside of sensorimotor cortex contralateral to the utilized limb was effective in evoking the behavior in the no cue/no pellet condition (ipsilateral sensorimotor, 0/68 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 4G; frontal, 0/20 trials, n = 2 animals; visual, 0/21 trials, n = 3 animals).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=3 animals and reference to Figure 4G.

claim: Inhibition of frontal cortex did not evoke rebound prehension (0/20 trials, n = 2 animals).
source: Rebound prehension showed dependence on a number of factors. Anatomically, no area outside of sensorimotor cortex contralateral to the utilized limb was effective in evoking the behavior in the no cue/no pellet condition (ipsilateral sensorimotor, 0/68 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 4G; frontal, 0/20 trials, n = 2 animals; visual, 0/21 trials, n = 3 animals).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=2 animals.

claim: Inhibition of visual cortex did not evoke rebound prehension (0/21 trials, n = 3 animals).
source: Rebound prehension showed dependence on a number of factors. Anatomically, no area outside of sensorimotor cortex contralateral to the utilized limb was effective in evoking the behavior in the no cue/no pellet condition (ipsilateral sensorimotor, 0/68 trials, n = 3 animals, Figure 4G; frontal, 0/20 trials, n = 2 animals; visual, 0/21 trials, n = 3 animals).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=3 animals.

claim: At least 2 s (median across animals) of cortical inhibition was required to achieve rebound prehension rates above 90% (n = 4 animals).
source: Duration of cortical inhibition was also a critical factor in initiating rebound prehension. At least 2 s (median across animals) of cortical inhibition was required to achieve rebound prehension rates above 90% (n = 4 animals, Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=4 animals and reference to Figure 4H.

claim: Longer durations (4 s was longest tested) of cortical inhibition reduced the latency variability of prehension initiation (n = 2 animals).
source: Longer durations (4 s was longest tested) of cortical inhibition also reduced the latency variability of prehension initiation (n = 2 animals, Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=2 animals and reference to Figure 4H.

claim: Long durations of photostimulation (2 s or more) were specifically associated with prominent rebound spiking in cortical neurons.
source: Interestingly, long durations of photostimulation (2 s or more) were specifically associated with prominent rebound spiking in cortical neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rebound spiking in the cortex may be responsible for rebound prehension.
source: This raises the possibility that rebound spiking in the cortex is responsible for rebound prehension.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Rebound prehension itself is cortically dependent, as reactivation of sensorimotor inhibitory cortical neurons freezes progression of the rebound movement.
source: Rebound prehension itself is also cortically dependent, as reactivation of sensorimotor inhibitory cortical neurons freezes progression of the rebound movement (Videos 19, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Videos 19 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The presence of food in the mouth decreased rebound prehension rates (18/95 trials exhibited rebound).
source: The presence of food in the mouth decreased rebound prehension rates (18/95 trials exhibited rebound; Figure 4I; Videos 11, 13–15).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 4I and Videos 11, 13–15.

claim: For nearly all trials with food in the mouth (93/95), animals were still chewing at light termination.
source: For nearly all of these (93/95) trials, animals were still chewing at light termination.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: Prehension generally occurred (21/29 trials) if the light was terminated during pelletless chewing.
source: To distinguish whether the reduced rate of rebound prehension was related to motor-program competition (chewing versus prehension) or to motivation (due to consumption of the pellet), we assayed rebound rates for failure trials where animals were chewing without the pellet (29/256 trials, Figure 4I). Prehension generally occurred (21/29 trials) if the light was terminated during pelletless chewing.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 4I.

claim: Animals on free food for one day exhibited significantly reduced rates of rebound prehension despite still engaging in the control version of the behavior.
source: To further test the role of hunger/satiety, we terminated food deprivation; animals on free food for one day exhibited significantly reduced rates of rebound prehension despite still engaging in the control version of the behavior (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 4J.

claim: Motivational drive, operating along both short (eating) and long (sated) time scales, gates rebound prehension.
source: These results suggest that motivational drive, operating along both short (eating) and long (sated) time scales, gates rebound prehension.

claim: Evocation of the learned behavior depends on features of the inhibition.

claim: Cortex is necessary for initiating and executing the dexterous and non-dexterous steps of skilled movement.
source: Contrary to the view that cortex is only involved in achieving dexterity (Kawai et al., 2015), we found cortex to be necessary for initiating and executing the dexterous and non-dexterous steps of this skilled movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings with citation.

claim: The necessity of cortex for initiation and execution is consistent with some interpretations of experiments where cortical stimulation delayed or interrupted voluntary movements in primates.
source: The necessity of cortex for initiation and execution is consistent with some interpretations of experiments where cortical stimulation delayed or interrupted voluntary movements in primates (Penfield and Jasper, 1954; Day et al., 1989; Lemon et al., 1995; Churchland and Shenoy, 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work with citation support.

claim: Previous activation studies of cortex have shown that electrical stimulation for behaviorally relevant durations produces motor sequences.
source: Previous activation studies of cortex have shown that electrical (Ferrier, 1873; Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Penfield, 1954; Gottlieb et al., 1993; Graziano et al., 2002; Ramanathan et al., 2006; Bonazzi et al., 2013) and optogenetic (Harrison et al., 2012) stimulation for behaviorally relevant durations produces motor sequences.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

source: Previous activation studies of cortex have shown that electrical (Ferrier, 1873; Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Penfield, 1954; Gottlieb et al., 1993; Graziano et al., 2002; Ramanathan et al., 2006; Bonazzi et al., 2013) and optogenetic (Harrison et al., 2012) stimulation for behaviorally relevant durations produces motor sequences.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Rebound prehension is a coordinated sequence of movements (reaching, grabbing, and eating) accurately directed to an external goal regardless of starting position.
source: Rebound prehension differs from these movements in three ways: rebound prehension is a coordinated sequence of movements (reaching, grabbing, and eating) accurately directed to an external goal regardless of starting position, depends on training, and is gated by motivation (Ramanathan et al., 2006; Harrison et al., 2012; Bonazzi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental findings with citation support.

claim: Rebound prehension depends on training.
source: Rebound prehension differs from these movements in three ways: rebound prehension is a coordinated sequence of movements (reaching, grabbing, and eating) accurately directed to an external goal regardless of starting position, depends on training, and is gated by motivation (Ramanathan et al., 2006; Harrison et al., 2012; Bonazzi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental findings with citation support.

claim: Rebound prehension is gated by motivation.
source: Rebound prehension differs from these movements in three ways: rebound prehension is a coordinated sequence of movements (reaching, grabbing, and eating) accurately directed to an external goal regardless of starting position, depends on training, and is gated by motivation (Ramanathan et al., 2006; Harrison et al., 2012; Bonazzi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental findings with citation support.

claim: Termination of inhibition evokes a motor engram specifying a learned goal/end-point of a trained behavior.
source: These differences suggest that termination of inhibition evokes a motor engram specifying a learned goal/end-point of a trained behavior (Bernstein, 1967; Todorov and Jordan, 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings with citation support.

source: Cortical synapses modified during the learning of skilled actions (Rioult-Pedotti et al., 1998; Xu et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011) may be responsible for the formation of these motor engrams.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation support.

source: Alternatively, the engram could be stored elsewhere, and relief of cortical inhibition could trigger or permit its activation in a downstream network.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation.

source: Mice were initially trained for approximately 30 min per day, until they started licking pellets (10 or 20 mg; Test Diet; St Louis, MO) placed directly below their mouth.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: Food pellets arrived ~ 200 ms after the start of an auditory tone (5 kHz).
source: Food pellets arrived ~ 200 ms after the start of an auditory tone (5 kHz) by rotating the turntable with a servomotor driven by custom-programmed Arduino software.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: After mastering the task (approximately 15 sessions), turntable placement was reproduced daily for each animal by aligning live images to a reference image.
source: After mastering the task (approximately 15 sessions), turntable placement was reproduced daily for each animal by aligning live images to a reference image.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: Inter-trial intervals ranged from 20 s to 1 min and approximately 50 trials were collected per day.
source: Inter-trial intervals ranged from 20 s to 1 min and approximately 50 trials were collected per day.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: Two high-speed, high-resolution monochrome cameras captured at 500 frames/s at a resolution of 352 × 260 pixels.
source: Two high-speed, high-resolution monochrome cameras (Point Grey Flea3; 1.3 MP Mono USB3 Vision VITA 1300; Point Grey Research Inc.; Richmond, BC, Canada) with 6–15 mm (f/1.4) lenses (C-Mount; Tokina, Japan) were placed perpendicularly in front and to the right of the animal. A custom-made near-infrared LED light source was mounted on each camera. Cameras were synced to each other and captured at 500 frames/s at a resolution of 352 × 260 pixels.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental equipment and procedures.

claim: A 473 nm laser was used to excite ChR2 in cortical inhibitory interneurons.
source: To excite ChR2 in cortical inhibitory interneurons through either a cranial window or cleared skulls of Slc32a1-COP4*H134R/EYFP mice, we used a 200 μm core, 0.39 numerical aperture fiber (FT200UMT; Thorlabs Inc; Newton, New Jersey) and a fiber-coupled 473 nm laser (LuxX 473–80; Omicron Laserage; Rodgau-Dudenhofen, Germany).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental equipment and procedures.

claim: 40 Hz sinusoidal stimulation with average power of 1–15 mW at the fiber's end was delivered for 0.1–4 s.
source: 40 Hz sinusoidal stimulation with average power of 1–15 mW at the fiber's end was delivered for 0.1–4 s, and power was reduced to 0 mW over the final 100 ms of stimulation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: Laser power of 10–15 mW has been shown to silence spike rates by 90% within 1.5 mm of the center of the laser spot.
source: Laser power of 10–15 mW has been shown to silence spike rates by 90% within 1.5 mm of the center of the laser spot (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: During testing, trials with optogenetic perturbation were interleaved with control trials without laser stimulation (< 20% laser trials, randomly interspersed).
source: During testing, trials with optogenetic perturbation were interleaved with control trials without laser stimulation (< 20% laser trials, randomly interspersed).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: The Slc32a1-COP4*H134R/EYFP mouse line expresses ChR2 in a small set of striatal neurons.
source: The Slc32a1-COP4*H134R/EYFP mouse line used in this study expresses ChR2 in a small set of striatal neurons (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: At the depths (+1.8mm) of the striatum, the intensity of the 473 nm light is negligible using the experimental strategy.
source: We directly measured the transmission of blue light through the cortex into the striatum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). At the depths (+1.8mm) of the striatum, the intensity of the 473 nm light is negligible using our experimental strategy.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Delivery of 473 nm light to striatum did not halt prehension behavior (prehension initiation in 190/191 laser trials versus 271/271 control trials) in three trained Slc32a1-COP4*H134R/EYFP mice.
source: We also implanted fibers into striatum (FT200UMT; Thorlabs Inc; Newton, New Jersey; coordinates: 1.7 mm lateral of midline; 0.5 mm anterior of bregma; 2.25 mm deep of brain surface) of three trained Slc32a1-COP4*H134R/EYFP mice. Delivery of 473 nm light did not halt prehension behavior (prehension initiation in 190/191 laser trials versus 271/271 control trials) in any of these animals.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: It is very unlikely that activation of striatal neurons is responsible for the behavioral phenotypes described in this paper.
source: Therefore, it is very unlikely that activation of striatal neurons is responsible for the behavioral phenotypes described in this paper.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Photostimulation produced prehension deficits in mice (n = 2 animals) where viral injection limited ChR2 expression to sensorimotor cortical neurons.
source: However, using photostimulation, we were able to produce prehension deficits in mice (n = 2 animals, mouse 1 exhibited prehension initiation in 1/24 laser trials versus 69/72 control trials, mouse 2 exhibited prehension initiation in 11/21 laser trials versus 67/67 control trials) where viral injection limited ChR2 expression to sensorimotor cortical neurons (AAV 2/1 or 2/7 Synapsin-FLEX-REV-ChR2, 5 sites in sensorimotor (forelimb) cortex, depths of 300 and 600 μm) in Gad2-IRES-Cre (Stock number: 010802; The Jackson Laboratory; Bar Harbor, ME) mice.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with n=2 animals.

claim: ChR2-positive axons were not detected in the external capsule or corpus callosum of Slc32a1-COP4*H134R/EYFP mice.
source: We also did not detect ChR2-positive axons in the external capsule or corpus callosum of Slc32a1-COP4*H134R/EYFP mice (data not shown), further ruling out the possibility that long range cortical inputs and outputs mediate the reported phenotypes.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: The authors developed a machine-learning-based method to automatically track the mouse's utilized hand using a modified version of Cascaded Pose Regression.
source: To quantitatively compare tone-cued (control) and laser-evoked (rebound) prehension, we developed a machine-learning-based method to automatically track the mouse's utilized hand. We manually labeled the position of the hand in a small subset of video frames, then used a modified version of Cascaded Pose Regression (Burgos-Artizzu et al., 2013) to learn a function that could input a frame and automatically predict the position of the hand in that frame.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods with citation support.

claim: Cascaded Pose Regression operates directly on a single video frame, and learns a cascade of multiple regressors, which each iteratively bring the target position estimate closer to the ground-truth labels.
source: Cascaded Pose Regression operates directly on a single video frame, and learns a cascade of multiple regressors, which each iteratively bring the target position estimate closer to the ground-truth labels.
evidence: This is a description of the computational method.

claim: The authors reconstructed three-dimensional trajectories by calibrating the cameras using the Camera Calibration Toolbox for MATLAB.
source: Using the two-dimensional (2D) trajectories corresponding to the front and side view videos, we reconstructed the three-dimensional trajectories by calibrating the cameras using the Camera Calibration Toolbox for MATLAB (J.-Y. Bouguet, http://www.vision.caltech.edu/bouguetj/calib_doc/ [2004]).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods with citation support.

claim: Extracellular spikes were recorded from Slc32a1-COP4*H134R/EYFP mice (n = 2) using silicon probes.
source: Extracellular spikes were recorded from Slc32a1-COP4*H134R/EYFP mice (n = 2) using silicon probes (A4 × 8-5 mm-100-200-177; NeuroNexus; Ann Arbor, MI) (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods with n=2 mice and citation support.

claim: Eighty-seven single units were recorded under awake, non-behaving conditions.
source: Eighty-seven single units were recorded under awake, non-behaving conditions.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: Units with spike width <0.35 ms were defined as fast spiking neurons (10/90).
source: For each unit, spike width was computed as the trough-to-peak interval in the mean spike waveform. Units with spike width <0.35 ms were defined as fast spiking neurons (10/90) and units with spike width >0.45 ms were defined as putative pyramidal neurons (77/90) (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods with citation support.

claim: Units with spike width >0.45 ms were defined as putative pyramidal neurons (77/90).
source: For each unit, spike width was computed as the trough-to-peak interval in the mean spike waveform. Units with spike width <0.35 ms were defined as fast spiking neurons (10/90) and units with spike width >0.45 ms were defined as putative pyramidal neurons (77/90) (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods with citation support.
